stories.headline: Hungary's New Prime Minister Péter Magyar to Be Sworn In, Ending 16 Years of Orbán Rule
stories.summary:
Hungary's new prime minister Péter Magyar is set to be sworn in Saturday after his Tisza party won a landslide election victory last month, capturing 141 of 199 parliamentary seats after being founded just two years ago. The inauguration caps a dramatic political shift that ended Viktor Orbán's 16-year grip on power, with Orbán's Fidesz party collapsing from 135 seats to 52. A large public celebration dubbed a "gateway of regime change" is planned along the Danube in Budapest.

Magyar has pledged a broad "change of system," promising to hold those responsible for financial crimes accountable while setting up a new office to recover what he describes as stolen state assets. Incoming ministers say there will be no political retribution, but investigations will proceed through proper legal channels. The incoming government is already facing a grim fiscal reality — a budget deficit swollen by a spending spree under the outgoing Orbán administration.

The transition has not been without controversy. Magyar's initial appointment of his brother-in-law as justice minister drew sharp criticism on social media; the nominee withdrew within days, saying he did not want "even the slightest shadow" cast on the new government. A prominent Fidesz-aligned businessman's large donation to Tisza was promptly returned by Magyar.

Orbán and most senior Fidesz figures have declined to take their parliamentary seats, leaving their political futures uncertain. The new government inherits a state whose contracts and public funds were widely funneled to Fidesz-linked business circles over more than a decade, according to incoming ministers — a pattern they say will now face scrutiny.

stories.headline: Canvas Cyberattack Disrupts Thousands of Schools Worldwide During Final Exams
stories.summary:
A cyberattack by the hacking group ShinyHunters knocked the Canvas online learning platform offline for much of Thursday and Friday, disrupting finals week for students at roughly 9,000 institutions across the United States, Canada, and Australia. The platform, owned by Instructure, is used by tens of millions of students and faculty to submit assignments, access course materials, and take exams. Several universities — including Mississippi State, Penn State, Idaho State, and the University of British Columbia — cancelled or postponed scheduled exams.

ShinyHunters claimed to have accessed billions of private messages and other records, and displayed ransom notes directly on students' screens during active exam sessions, demanding bitcoin payments in exchange for not releasing the data. Instructure confirmed the attackers exploited a vulnerability related to its Free-For-Teacher accounts and has temporarily shut down those accounts. The company has not disclosed whether any ransom was paid or what user data was compromised.

The breach caused widespread alarm during one of the highest-stakes periods of the academic calendar. Students mid-exam suddenly saw ransom messages appear and were left uncertain whether their completed work had been saved. Universities scrambled to communicate via email and alternative channels while advising students to log out and ignore suspicious messages.

The attack follows a pattern of escalating ransomware strikes on educational institutions, which hold large volumes of digitized personal and academic data. Previous attacks have targeted major school districts including Los Angeles Unified and Minneapolis Public Schools. Cybersecurity analysts note that schools remain attractive targets because of their data richness and historically limited security resources.

stories.headline: New U.S. Counterterrorism Strategy Targets Drug Cartels and Left-Wing Groups, Omits Right-Wing Extremism
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has released a 16-page national counterterrorism strategy that identifies three primary threats: narco-terrorists and transnational criminal gangs, legacy Islamist terrorist groups, and violent left-wing extremists including anarchists and anti-fascists. The document specifically cites "radically pro-transgender" ideology as a characteristic of the left-wing threat category, and references the suspect in the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The strategy makes no mention of right-wing or far-right extremist groups.

U.S. counterterrorism officials met Friday with allied nations to coordinate on the strategy's priorities. Administration officials argue the focus on cartels and gangs reflects the real-world threat posed by groups like the Sinaloa cartel and MS-13, which they say are pushing drugs and violence across U.S. borders. The document also addresses hostage recovery, terrorist acquisition of weapons of mass destruction, and the enduring threat from jihadist organizations.

Critics, including terrorism analysts, say the strategy has significant blind spots. Colin Clarke, executive director of The Soufan Center, said the omission of domestic far-right terrorism is a serious flaw, given that U.S. government research and independent studies have consistently found right-wing extremist groups responsible for the majority of violent domestic attacks in recent years. Clarke also described the document as "riddled with partisan accusations" despite its stated goal of being apolitical.

The debate over how to define and prioritize domestic terrorism threats has been politically charged for years. Conservatives have argued that previous administrations over-focused on right-wing threats while minimizing Islamist and left-wing violence; civil liberties groups and many security experts counter that data consistently shows far-right violence as the dominant domestic threat and warn that the new strategy politicizes what should be a data-driven process.

stories.headline: Mystery Naval Drone With Explosives Found in Greek Waters, Possibly Linked to Ukraine-Russia War
stories.summary:
Greek fishermen discovered an unmanned naval drone armed with explosives in a sea cave near the island of Lefkada in the Ionian Sea on Thursday, prompting the Greek coast guard to tow it to a nearby port. The Greek defence ministry is now overseeing an investigation into the drone's origin and purpose. Its engine was reportedly still running when it was found.

Greek media reports suggest the vessel may be Ukrainian-made or connected to the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. One newspaper identified it as resembling Ukraine's MAGURA V5 naval drone, which has been used in multiple attacks on Russian warships and oil tankers. That identification has not been independently verified, and neither Greece's nor Ukraine's military has officially commented.

Investigators are working to determine whether the drone ended up in Greek territorial waters due to a technical failure, a loss of communication with its operators, or another cause. One theory under examination is that it may have been deployed against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" — the network of tankers used to transport Russian oil in circumvention of Western sanctions.

The incident highlights the expanding geographic reach of the naval drone campaign that Ukraine has waged since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian sea drones have previously struck Russian vessels in the Black Sea, the Mediterranean, and other distant waters. The presence of such a weapon in Greek territorial waters raises sensitive questions about the spread of the conflict's military hardware into neutral EU member states.

stories.headline: Judge Rules Trump's DOGE-Led Cancellation of Humanities Grants Unconstitutional
stories.summary:
A federal judge in New York permanently barred the Trump administration from terminating more than $100 million in National Endowment for the Humanities grants, ruling Thursday that the cancellations violated the First and Fifth Amendments. U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon found that the Department of Government Efficiency had no lawful authority to end the congressionally approved funding, which covered more than 1,400 grants to scholars, writers, research groups and other organizations.

McMahon wrote that officials engaged in 'a textbook example of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination' by canceling grants associated with diversity, equity and inclusion, and criticized DOGE's use of artificial intelligence in making the cuts. The ruling sided with plaintiffs including The Authors Guild, the American Historical Association, the Modern Language Association and individual grant recipients who sued DOGE and the NEH.

Government lawyers had argued the cuts were legal exercises of executive authority to eliminate DEI-linked programs and reduce discretionary spending. The White House and Justice Department did not immediately comment, and it was unclear whether an appeal was planned.

The decision is the latest in a series of judicial checks on DOGE-driven spending cuts. Supporters of the ruling called it a vindication of free speech and congressional appropriations authority; the administration has argued across similar cases that the president holds broad discretion to realign federal spending with executive priorities.

stories.headline: Update: Court Again Strikes Down Trump's Global Tariffs; Administration Appeals
stories.summary:
The U.S. Court of International Trade issued a 2-to-1 ruling Thursday declaring the Trump administration's 10% global import tariff unauthorized by law, finding that the White House misinterpreted Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 and failed to satisfy the legal criteria for such surcharges. The court ordered that illegally collected tariffs 'shall be refunded with interest,' mirroring an earlier Supreme Court ruling that struck down Trump's 'Liberation Day' tariffs imposed under separate emergency powers.

The Trump administration appealed the ruling Friday, which may delay any immediate halt to tariff collection by 30 days or more. The 10% Section 122 duties had been put in place as a temporary replacement for the previously invalidated Liberation Day tariffs and were scheduled to expire July 24 regardless.

The administration had planned to replace the temporary duties with permanent tariffs under Section 301 and Section 232 authorities, but the lengthy investigation process required means those measures are unlikely to take effect for months, leaving a window in which importers could again accelerate purchases to avoid future duties — a pattern seen before the original Liberation Day announcement.

President Trump blasted the decision as the work of 'two radical left judges.' Economists at Capital Economics noted the ruling may not immediately change the effective U.S. tariff rate but raises the risk of further Treasury refund obligations and signals continued judicial resistance to the administration's broader trade agenda.

stories.headline: Justice Department Moves to Strip 12 Americans of Citizenship Over Fraud Allegations
stories.summary:
The Department of Justice announced Friday it is seeking to denaturalize a dozen people across the country whom federal prosecutors accuse of fraudulently obtaining U.S. citizenship by lying during the naturalization process. Actions were filed this week in U.S. District Courts in multiple jurisdictions.

Among those targeted is former U.S. Ambassador Victor Manuel Rocha, against whom the DOJ filed a complaint in the Southern District of Florida alleging he illegally obtained naturalization by misrepresenting himself while serving as a spy for the Cuban government. The other 11 individuals face allegations including child sexual abuse and providing material support to terrorist organizations.

The move is part of the Trump administration's broader effort to use denaturalization as an enforcement tool, an authority that has historically been used sparingly. Immigration advocates have raised concerns that expanding its use could create uncertainty for naturalized citizens more broadly, while administration officials argue the actions target individuals who obtained citizenship through deliberate deception.

Denaturalization cases are decided in federal civil court and require the government to prove fraud by clear and convincing evidence. The cases announced Friday represent one of the largest single-day batches of such filings in recent memory.

stories.headline: David Attenborough Turns 100 as World Celebrates His Seven Decades of Nature Broadcasting
stories.summary:
Sir David Attenborough, the BBC broadcaster whose narration of nature documentaries spanning more than 70 years shaped global public understanding of the natural world, turned 100 on Friday. The BBC hosted a celebration at the Royal Albert Hall, cinemas screened his films, and scientists, politicians and conservationists worldwide offered tributes to a career that took viewers from the Himalayas to the Amazon.

Attenborough was born in London on May 8, 1926, and built a body of work that includes landmark series such as Life on Earth, The Private Life of Plants and The Blue Planet. Colleagues described him as insistent that the animals, not he, were the stars of his programs, and uncomfortable with personal fame despite being one of the most recognized voices on the planet.

Over time, Attenborough moved from neutral observer to outspoken advocate on climate change, ocean plastic and biodiversity loss — a shift his collaborators say was driven by frustration that political and business leaders were not responding to mounting scientific evidence. Evolutionary biologist Professor Ben Garrod noted that Attenborough 'shouldn't have ever had to have turned to policymaking and advocacy.'

Alastair Fothergill, producer of several of Attenborough's most celebrated series, said Attenborough maintained through his career that scientific accuracy was as important as stunning imagery, helping audiences understand not only the beauty of the natural world but the reasons to protect it.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Accuses U.S. of 'Reckless Military Adventure' as Naval Clashes Continue, Deal Response Due
stories.summary:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the United States on Friday of pursuing a "reckless military adventure" each time a diplomatic solution is within reach, posting on X that Iranians would "never bow to pressure." The statement came a day after both sides accused each other of initiating attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and as U.S. Central Command announced it had disabled two Iranian-flagged oil tankers attempting to enter an Iranian port on the Gulf of Oman by firing precision munitions into their smokestacks. Centcom said U.S. forces are currently preventing more than 70 tankers from entering or leaving Iranian ports under an ongoing naval blockade.

Despite the exchanges, President Trump maintained that the ceasefire enabling diplomatic talks remains intact. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking during a visit to Italy, said Iran is expected to respond to U.S. proposals on Friday, adding: "I hope it's a serious offer, I really do." The conflict, now in its third month following the U.S.-Israeli military campaign launched in February, has choked the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas normally transits.

Iran's Foreign Minister framed the continued military action as potentially the work of a "spoiler" manipulating the U.S. president, questioning whether the strikes were a pressure tactic or evidence that Trump was being "duped into another quagmire." Trump, for his part, posted to Truth Social that U.S. forces had destroyed multiple Iranian small boats, missiles and drones, and warned of stronger action if Iran continued to engage. The dueling accusations underscore the precarious state of ceasefire-backed negotiations.

The standoff carries significant global economic consequences. Jet fuel prices in Europe have surged roughly 50 percent since the conflict began, and energy markets remain volatile. With Iran's expected diplomatic response due Friday and U.S. forces actively interdicting vessels, the next 24 to 48 hours are widely seen as critical to determining whether talks advance or the conflict escalates further.

stories.headline: Update: Comey Trial Set for July 15 on Charges Stemming from Trump Threat Allegation
stories.summary:
A federal judge on Friday scheduled a criminal trial for former FBI Director James Comey to begin July 15, setting in motion one of the most politically charged prosecutions of the Trump era. U.S. District Judge Louise Flanagan will preside over the case in her North Carolina courtroom. Comey was charged with threatening the president after posting a photograph of seashells arranged on a beach, which prosecutors allege constituted a veiled death threat against Trump.

The judge also agreed that Comey would not be required to appear in person at a Monday procedural hearing. Comey has denied that the post carried any threatening intent, and his defense is expected to argue the charges represent a politically motivated prosecution brought by a Justice Department serving under a president Comey investigated during his tenure as FBI director.

Supporters of the charges contend the law must apply equally regardless of political status, while critics — including civil liberties advocates and former law enforcement officials — have characterized the prosecution as an unprecedented use of federal criminal statutes to target a political adversary over an ambiguous social media post. The case has drawn intense scrutiny as a test of the independence of the federal judiciary and the boundaries of protected speech.

Comey led the FBI from 2013 until Trump fired him in 2017, an event that contributed to the appointment of Special Counsel Robert Mueller. The trial date places the proceedings in the middle of a congressional election season, guaranteeing sustained national attention.

stories.headline: Japan's Largest Anti-War Protests in Decades Erupt as PM Pushes Military Expansion
stories.summary:
Japan is experiencing its largest anti-war protests in decades as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who took office in October 2025, advances a sweeping departure from the country's postwar pacifist doctrine. Since coming to power, Takaichi has lifted longstanding restrictions on arms exports and expanded Japan's military role abroad, arguing that an assertive China, unpredictable North Korea, and nearby Russia demand a more capable defense posture. On April 21, the government took the significant step of lifting Japan's ban on exporting lethal weapons.

Thousands of demonstrators gathered outside the prime minister's office in Tokyo and at other locations, carrying placards calling for the preservation of Article 9 of Japan's 1947 constitution, which renounces war and prohibits the maintenance of armed forces. Protesters spanned generations, with many participants in their twenties and thirties, signaling that pacifist sentiment is not confined to those with direct memory of World War Two. "I'm angry that these changes could be made without properly listening to us," said one 30-year-old demonstrator.

The government frames its security pivot as a necessary response to regional realities and to pressure from Washington, which has urged Tokyo to assume a more active role in collective defense. Takaichi is not the first conservative leader to challenge Article 9 — former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe passed legislation in 2015 allowing limited collective self-defense — but her moves are seen as more sweeping than those of her predecessors.

The protests signal a deepening tension at the heart of Japanese national identity, pitting a constitutional pacifism enshrined after devastating defeat in 1945 against the strategic imperatives of an increasingly militarized Indo-Pacific. How Takaichi responds to the public pressure, and whether she pursues a formal constitutional amendment, will have significant implications for regional security alliances and the balance of power in Asia.

stories.headline: Update: Two IS-Linked Australian Women Charged with Crimes Against Humanity After Returning from Syria
stories.summary:
Three Australian women with alleged ties to the Islamic State appeared in Australian courts on Friday, less than 24 hours after being arrested upon their return from Syria. Kawsar Ahmad, 53, faces four charges of crimes against humanity, with police alleging she traveled to Syria in 2014 and kept a female slave in her home; her daughter Zeinab Ahmad, 31, faces two similar charges carrying a maximum sentence of 25 years. A third woman, Janai Safar, 32, appeared in a Sydney court charged with entering a declared conflict zone and joining IS, offenses carrying up to ten years in prison.

The Australian Federal Police allege Kawsar Ahmad was complicit in the purchase of a female slave for $10,000 USD and that both mother and daughter knowingly kept the woman in their home. Kawsar and Zeinab Ahmad were remanded in custody until Monday, when their lawyers said they would seek bail; Safar was also remanded and will next appear in court in July.

The three women are part of a larger group of 34 Australian women and children who had been held at the al-Roj camp in northeast Syria since 2019. The cohort had attempted to return to Australia earlier in the year but were sent back to the camp for what the government described as "technical reasons," with authorities refusing to offer repatriation assistance.

AFP Assistant Commissioner for Counter Terrorism Stephen Nutt said the investigation into Australians who traveled to declared conflict areas remains active and that authorities "will ensure those who are alleged to have committed a criminal offence are put before the courts." The charges mark one of the most significant terrorism-related prosecutions in Australia in recent years.

stories.headline: Update: EU and Aviation Bodies Clear Use of U.S.-Grade Jet Fuel in Europe Amid Iran War Supply Crunch
stories.summary:
The European Union, the International Air Transport Association (IATA), and the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday moved to ease potential aviation fuel shortages in Europe caused by disruptions to Gulf supplies stemming from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The EU stated there are no "regulatory obstacles" to European airlines using American-grade Jet A fuel, provided it is introduced safely, while EASA issued a formal safety information bulletin with guidance for fuel suppliers, airlines, and airport operators.

The price of Jet A-1, the international standard fuel used by most European carriers, has risen approximately 50 percent since the conflict began, as supplies from the Gulf region have slowed sharply. IATA's director of flight and technical operations warned that if the Middle East conflict continues, "it won't be long before we see fuel shortages in some parts of the world."

The two fuel types — Jet A-1 and the North American Jet A — are both kerosene-based and broadly similar, but Jet A-1 has a lower freezing point, making it more flexible for long-haul and polar routes. EASA cautioned that introducing Jet A without careful management "could result in an aircraft flying outside of its safe operating limits," particularly if fuel grades are inconsistently available across airports.

The regulatory move represents a significant practical response to wartime supply chain disruption, with European carriers now able to tap increased U.S. refinery output to offset the loss of Gulf imports. Industry officials said careful planning, monitoring, and the use of fuel additives — techniques already standard in cold-weather North American operations — can mitigate the technical risks involved.

stories.headline: Trump Meets Brazil's Lula at White House; No Joint Statement, but Trade Talks to Follow
stories.summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva held a three-hour meeting at the White House on Friday to discuss trade, tariffs, and bilateral relations. The meeting ended without a joint press appearance — unusual for a summit of this scale — as Lula's motorcade departed without either leader addressing reporters, leaving journalists who had waited hours without comment.

Trump posted on Truth Social afterward that the meeting "went very well" but offered few specifics. Brazilian ministers speaking at the Brazilian embassy echoed that characterization, saying representatives from both countries would meet in coming weeks to negotiate an end to U.S. tariffs on Brazilian goods. Lula told reporters separately that he had raised the idea of a transnational group to counter drug trafficking and organized crime, and that Brazil wished to share its critical rare earth mineral potential with interested investor nations.

The meeting carries diplomatic complexity: Trump has a close relationship with Lula's predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whom he had publicly backed for re-election. Bolsonaro is currently imprisoned in Brazil after being convicted of attempting to stage a coup to remain in power. When asked whether Trump might seek to influence Brazil's upcoming elections, Lula said: "I don't think Trump will have any influence."

The encounter is the latest in a series of White House meetings with foreign leaders as the Trump administration pursues bilateral trade negotiations following its sweeping tariff actions. Brazil is a major U.S. trading partner and one of the world's largest exporters of agricultural commodities, making any tariff resolution economically significant for both countries.

stories.headline: U.S. Economy Added 115,000 Jobs in April, Nearly Double Expectations
stories.summary:
The U.S. economy added 115,000 jobs in April, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, far exceeding economists' consensus forecast of roughly 65,000 to 67,000 new positions. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.3 percent. The report marked the first back-to-back monthly advance in hiring in nearly a year.

The stronger-than-expected figures suggest the labor market retains meaningful resilience despite ongoing uncertainty tied to tariff policy and elevated interest rates. Economists had broadly anticipated a sharper slowdown in hiring given the macroeconomic headwinds facing employers. The results prompted U.S. stocks to approach record closing highs, with semiconductor shares and the holding of the Iran ceasefire also contributing to market gains.

The report will factor heavily into Federal Reserve deliberations over the pace and timing of any interest rate adjustments. Policymakers have signaled they want sustained evidence that inflation and employment conditions justify cuts before moving. Friday's numbers reduce pressure on the Fed to act quickly but also complicate the case for those arguing the tariff environment has already begun materially damaging the labor market.

The April data will be scrutinized by both political parties. Supporters of the current administration are likely to point to the beat as evidence of economic durability, while critics will note the unemployment rate remains elevated compared to the historic lows recorded in 2023 and that the pace of hiring has slowed considerably from prior years.

stories.headline: Update: Farage's Reform UK Sweeps English Local Elections, Delivering Major Blow to Starmer's Labour
stories.summary:
Nigel Farage's populist Reform UK party posted sweeping gains in English local elections, winning more than 400 council races and dealing a significant defeat to Prime Minister Keir Starmer's Labour government in results reported Friday. The voting across England, Scotland and Wales represented the largest electoral test for Starmer since Labour won the general election in 2024.

Starmer said he had no intention of stepping down as Labour leader despite the scale of the losses, acknowledging that voters were sending a message of dissatisfaction but framing the results as a reflection of difficult decisions his government has had to make in office. Reform UK, which campaigns on strict immigration controls, opposition to net-zero climate policies and skepticism of mainstream political institutions, has rapidly consolidated support that previously flowed to both the Conservative Party and disaffected Labour voters.

The results mark a significant milestone for Farage, who has sought to position Reform as the primary opposition force in British politics ahead of the next general election. The Conservatives, who lost power in 2024, also suffered losses, reinforcing questions about whether the party can recover its traditional base or whether Reform has permanently fractured the British right.

Analysts cautioned that local election results do not translate directly to general election outcomes, but the breadth of Reform's gains — across regions that historically voted Labour as well as Conservative — indicates the party's appeal extends well beyond its initial base of Brexit-aligned voters in English towns and coastal communities.

stories.headline: Three Hikers Killed After Volcano Erupts on Indonesian Island Despite Warnings
stories.summary:
Three hikers — two Singaporeans and one Indonesian — died Friday after Mount Dukono on North Maluku island erupted during an early morning hike, sending a column of ash 10 kilometers into the sky. The three were among a group of approximately 20 Singaporeans and Indonesians climbing the mountain in defiance of official restrictions. The remaining members of the group were located and evacuated to hospital.

Indonesian authorities said retrieval of the bodies was hampered by repeated eruptions, difficult terrain and strong volcanic blasts. A rescue operation to reach the crater, where the bodies are believed to be located, was suspended as darkness fell Friday evening and is set to resume Saturday. The volcano was still emitting ash and rock material from its crater late Friday afternoon.

Mount Dukono has erupted more than 200 times since March of last year, and officials had issued and widely publicized warnings — including on social media and via banners at trailheads — against climbing the mountain. A guide who was on the mountain with clients at the time of the eruption told BBC Indonesian that he sensed pressure building inside the volcano and descended quickly, saving his group.

The deaths underscore the dangers posed by active volcanoes in the Indonesian archipelago, which sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire and is home to dozens of highly active volcanic peaks. Officials said eyewitness accounts suggest additional hikers beyond the identified group of 20 were also on the mountain at the time of the eruption.

stories.headline: Pentagon Releases New Tranche of UFO Files Under Trump Transparency Order
stories.summary:
The Pentagon released a new batch of classified files on unidentified anomalous phenomena, commonly known as UFOs or UAPs, on Friday as part of President Trump's directive ordering the Defense Department to make such documents public. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in a statement that the documents "have long fueled justified speculation" and that it was time for the American public to see them.

The release follows a 2024 congressional report that catalogued hundreds of new UAP incidents but found no confirmed evidence that the U.S. government had ever verified a sighting of alien technology. Experts said the newly released files could help scientists and researchers shed light on unexplained aerial incidents and longstanding questions about government secrecy surrounding the topic.

The Trump administration has positioned transparency on UAPs as a bipartisan priority, building on disclosure legislation passed by Congress in recent years that sought to compel executive-branch agencies to declassify and release historical records on the subject. The Pentagon has previously acknowledged operating programs that investigated UAP reports going back decades.

The scope and content of Friday's document release were not fully detailed in early reporting, and analysts cautioned that official document dumps have historically contained heavily redacted materials. Independent researchers and advocacy groups have called for the release of unredacted files and raw sensor data to allow independent verification of government claims.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Pauses Iran Military Operation as Ceasefire Holds Tenuously; Israel Strikes Beirut
stories.summary:
President Trump announced a pause in U.S. military operations against Iran — dubbed 'Project Freedom' — saying progress has been made toward a deal. The pause comes two days after Trump announced the operation and follows intensive diplomatic activity, including Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi holding talks in Beijing with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on his first visit to China since the war began.

Despite the pause, tensions remain high. Iran accused the U.S. of violating the ceasefire by targeting an oil tanker and striking coastal areas. The U.S. maintained it had targeted Iranian 'missile and drone launch sites, command and control locations, and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance nodes.' The fragile Gulf ceasefire is under serious strain from continued U.S.-Iran exchanges.

Israel carried out a strike on Beirut targeting a senior Hezbollah figure — the first such strike on the Lebanese capital since mid-April — even as a U.S.-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah nominally remains in effect. Israeli media also reported that Israel is preparing to resume full-scale fighting in Gaza due to an impasse in disarmament talks with Hamas.

Mediator Pakistan said it is 'endeavouring to convert this ceasefire into a permanent end to this war,' but analysts warn the dual fronts in Lebanon and Iran, combined with the stalled Gaza negotiations, make a durable peace elusive. European aviation authorities separately warned that jet fuel shortages tied to the conflict could worsen if fighting continues.

stories.headline: Russia Escalating Foreign Assassination Campaign Since Ukraine Invasion, Western Officials Say
stories.summary:
Three Western intelligence officials from separate countries have told the Associated Press that Russia has significantly ramped up a campaign of targeted killings abroad since President Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Officials say Russia's security services have become more brazen, now targeting not only Russian dissidents but also foreign supporters of Ukraine, including arms company executives and military officials.

Documented plots uncovered in recent years include: a suspected reconnaissance operation outside a Russian activist's home in France in April 2025; disrupted assassination plots in Lithuania against a Ukrainian supporter and a Russian activist; two foiled plots in Germany targeting a weapons company executive and a Ukrainian military official; and an arrest in Poland in 2024 linked to an alleged plot to kill Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. A Russian helicopter pilot who defected was killed in Spain, with Russian operatives considered prime suspects.

The AP used anonymous sourcing for the story, with the outlet's standards team explaining its policy. The Kremlin has consistently denied involvement in overseas killings, framing such allegations as Western disinformation. However, Western governments have repeatedly expelled Russian diplomats and sanctioned Russian intelligence officials in connection with the plots.

The report underscores the broader security challenge facing European governments as the war in Ukraine grinds on, with analysts warning that the boldness of Russian operations signals a deliberate strategy to intimidate critics and supporters of Kyiv across the continent.

stories.headline: Update: Third Briton Suspected of Hantavirus as Cruise Ship Outbreak Spreads; Passengers to Be Flown Home
stories.summary:
A third British national has developed a suspected hantavirus infection connected to the outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, the U.K. government confirmed Friday. The patient is currently on the remote Atlantic island of Tristan da Cunha, where the ship made a stop in mid-April. Five cases of hantavirus have now been confirmed overall, including one of three passengers who have died from the illness.

The MV Hondius is expected to dock in the Canary Islands this weekend, where a chartered British plane will meet the vessel to fly remaining U.K. passengers and crew home. Those returning will be asked to self-isolate for up to 45 days even if they display no symptoms. Two other confirmed British cases remain hospitalized — one in a stable condition in the Netherlands and one in intensive care in South Africa.

Contact tracing is under way across multiple countries, including Switzerland and the Netherlands, for dozens of passengers who disembarked before the outbreak was detected. The World Health Organization called the situation a 'serious incident' but said the risk to the general public remains low and stressed it bears no resemblance to the COVID-19 pandemic. The origin of the outbreak has not yet been determined.

Hantavirus is typically transmitted to humans through contact with infected rodents or their droppings and is not known to spread easily between people — a key distinction from respiratory illnesses. The unusual shipboard outbreak has prompted health authorities in several countries to issue monitoring and isolation guidance for former passengers.

stories.headline: Trump Administration to Begin Revoking Passports of Americans With Unpaid Child Support
stories.summary:
The U.S. State Department announced it will begin revoking passports of Americans who carry significant unpaid child support debt, targeting those with outstanding balances above $2,500. The department said it will work with the Department of Health and Human Services to identify delinquent parents. Those whose passports are revoked will be ineligible for new ones until their debt is cleared.

The policy expands enforcement of a rarely-used 1996 federal law. Previously, the consequence was applied only when parents with such debt sought to renew their passports; the new policy allows for proactive revocation. Americans abroad at the time of revocation will need to visit a U.S. embassy or consulate to obtain an emergency travel document to re-enter the country. The Associated Press reported enforcement is expected to begin Friday.

The State Department framed the action as using 'commonsense tools to support American families and strengthen compliance' with existing U.S. law, saying it enforces parents' 'legal and moral obligations to their children.' The department added that the action 'supports the welfare of American children by exacting real consequences for child support delinquency.'

Child support enforcement affects millions of American families; the federal Office of Child Support Services reported tens of billions of dollars in unpaid support owed nationally. The policy is expected to draw support from those who argue existing enforcement mechanisms are insufficient and criticism from civil liberties advocates concerned about the breadth of passport revocation as a collections tool.
